The fine-tuned encoder model demonstrated strong classification performance but may have been limited by potential inaccuracies in the registry reference standards during model training. This study further demonstrated the potential of LLMs in recovering plausible structured labels from narrative text, complementing cancer registries for metastasis ascertainment.

item.title: Midlife and Late-Life Alzheimer Disease Blood Biomarkers and 11-Year Cognitive Decline.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives Plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer disease (AD) neuropathology (amyloid-β42 to amyloid β40 [Aβ42/40] ratio, phosphorylated tau at threonine [p-tau181]), neurodegeneration (neurofilament light [NfL]), and neuroinflammation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) in late-life are associated with cognitive decline. Whether these biomarkers in midlife are predictive of subsequent cognitive decline, and whether they are associated with different cognitive domains, is uncertain. In this study, we investigated associations of midlife and late-life plasma Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP with late-life change in domain-specific (memory, language, and executive function) and global cognitive function. Methods We performed a prospective cohort analysis of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study (ARIC-NCS). Outcome follow-up was from ARIC visit 5 (2011-2013) to visit 9 (2021-2022). We included all individuals from ARIC field centers (Jackson, Mississippi; Forsyth County, North Carolina; Washington County, Maryland; and Minneapolis suburbs, Minnesota) with biomarkers measured from stored specimens in midlife (visit 3, 1993-1995, mean age 59.0 years) and late-life (visit 5, 2011-2013, mean age 76.8 years). Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were measured with the Quanterix Simoa platform and standardized to visit 3 to facilitate cross-biomarker comparisons of their rate of change from midlife to late-life. We estimated change in memory, language, executive function, and global cognition factor scores from visit 5 to visit 9 with linear mixed-effect models. Results In 1,515 included participants, 60.7% (n = 920) were female and 25.5% (n = 387) were Black. Each SD increase in p-tau181 in midlife was significantly associated with faster late-life memory decline (β = -0.030 [95% CI -0.059 to -0.001] SD. Midlife Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP were not associated with subsequent decline in any cognitive domain. In late-life, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were significantly associated with faster decline in different cognitive domains, with the strongest associations seen with memory (β = -0.091 [95% CI -0.123 to -0.058] SD; β = -0.064 [95% CI -0.106 to -0.023] SD; and β = -0.048 [95% CI -0.082 to -0.013] SD, respectively). Discussion Midlife p-tau181 was associated with faster 11-year memory decline beginning 20 years later in the ARIC cohort, which underscores a potentially long prodromal phase of cognitive decline that could precede dementia onset. In late-life, biomarkers for AD, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation were associated with faster decline across different cognitive domains, but associations remained strongest for p-tau181 and memory.

item.title: Multiscale neural signatures of long-lag repetition learning: a simultaneous fNIRS-EEG study.
item.description:
Neurophotonics
Significance Repetition-based learning supports word recognition and reading fluency, yet its neural mechanisms remain poorly understood, particularly where deficits in consolidating repeated linguistic input may underlie reading and language difficulties. Establishing reliable neural markers of repetition-based learning is a critical first step toward characterizing the phenotypes of these difficulties in children. Aim We developed a whole-brain simultaneous functional near-infrared spectroscopy-electroencephalography (fNIRS-EEG) approach to capture fast temporal electrophysiological and spatially accurate hemodynamic signals during long-lag repetition learning. Approach Thirty participants performed a semantic judgment task with words repeated across four runs with intervening items, modeling repetition demands central to reading instruction. A multimodal decoding framework integrating electrophysiological, hemodynamic, and cross-modal fNIRS-EEG correlation features was used to classify repetition-based learning. Results Repeated words showed response time reductions. EEG captured a frontal N400-range repetition-related negativity and attenuation of alpha-beta suppression, reflecting changes in recognition-related and post-recognition processing. fNIRS revealed left inferior frontal and superior temporal efficiency increases alongside right supramarginal activation, suggesting integrative processing. Multimodal classifiers outperformed unimodal classifiers, indicating that each modality captured complementary aspects of learning. Conclusions Combining fNIRS and EEG with multimodal machine learning provides a richer characterization of repetition-based learning than either modality alone, establishing a framework for phenotyping language learning capacity and identifying neural markers of reading difficulties in pediatric populations.

item.title: Involuntary facial muscle activity during imagined vocalisation contaminates EEG and enables emotion decoding.
item.description:
Journal of neural engineering
Objective. Decoding imagined speech from electroencephalography (EEG) recordings is potentially useful for brain-computer interfaces. Previous studies have focused on decoding semantic information from EEG, leaving the decoding of emotion - an important component of human communication - largely unexplored.Approach. Here, we report two experiments involving participants tasked with overt (n = 14) or imagined (n = 21) emotional vocalisation in five different categories: anger, happiness, neutral, sadness, and pleasure. Throughout, we recorded 64-channel EEG; we computed time-frequency features and used a logistic-regression classifier to evaluate emotion decoding accuracy. In five participants, we also recorded facial surface electromyography (sEMG) during imagined vocalisation, and studied the contamination of EEG by sEMG.Main results. Our results show that emotion can be decoded from single-trial EEG recordings of both overt (78.1%, chance = 20%) and imagined vocalisation (36.4%). The high-gamma band (50 to 100 Hz) and lateral EEG channels (T7, T8, and proximal) were important for decoding. sEMG analysis indicated that involuntary facial muscle activity contributed to these spectral and spatial patterns during imagined vocalisation. We identified a prominent muscle-induced pattern over lateral EEG channels - the railroad cross-tie pattern - showing greater activation during imagined happy vocalisations. We conclude that involuntary facial muscle activity is associated with certain emotion categories (i.e. happiness) and contributes to the decoding of emotion from single-trial EEG recordings.Significance. This study provides converging EEG and sEMG evidence demonstrating that involuntary facial muscle activity occurs during imagined vocalisation and is modulated by emotion, producing emotion-specific EEG contamination patterns. Although we focused on imagined vocalisations, the EMG patterns we observed closely resembled EEG patterns commonly reported in emotion decoding studies, raising concerns about involuntary facial muscle activity in such work.

item.title: Toward early dyslexia screening through handwriting: A trustworthy XAI-enhanced deep learning framework.
item.description:
Research in developmental disabilities
Dyslexia, a prevalent learning disorder, significantly impairs children's ability to process written language, often leading to challenges such as letter reversals, inconsistent spacing, and scrambled writing sequences. Early detection is critical for timely intervention, yet traditional diagnostic methods such as behavioral assessments and neuroimaging-are either time-consuming, subjective, or prohibitively expensive. Recent advances in deep learning offer promising alternatives, particularly through handwriting analysis, which is non-invasive and scalable. However, the "black-box" nature of many deep learning models raises concerns about interpretability, a key requirement for clinical and educational adoption. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework combining a custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and an Attention mechanism to detect dyslexia from handwriting samples. The study uses handwriting samples from adolescents aged 12-15 with an established dyslexia diagnosis and a control group. It therefore provides a proof-of-concept for handwriting-based classification and a foundation for early screening, rather than a validated early screening tool. The CNN extracts spatial features, while GRUs model temporal patterns in writing sequences. The Attention mechanism highlights the most discriminative regions for screening. To enhance transparency, Explainable AI (XAI) techniques such as Grad-CAM, LIME, and feature scatter plots are added to provide visual explanations of the model's decisions. Evaluated on a dataset of 3170 handwriting images from dyslexic and non-dyslexic students, the model achieved 99.5% accuracy using leave-one-out cross validation, outperforming pre-trained models like ResNet-50. Ablation studies confirmed the CNN's pivotal role while GRUs and Attention provided complementary improvements. These findings demonstrate technical feasibility; however, the model has not yet been evaluated in younger, undiagnosed children, and conclusions about early screening utility should therefore be interpreted with caution. XAI visualizations, such as Grad-CAM and LIME, offer interpretable saliency maps, and the results show that the predictions made by the model depend on the regions where known dyslexic characteristics, such as irregularities in letter curvature, spacing, and alignment, often occur.

item.title: Decoding Spatial Attention in the Cocktail Party Problem Using Whole-head High-Density fNIRS.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Spatial attention is critical for solving the cocktail party problem, a longstanding problem in neuroscience and artificial speech recognition. The ability to decode where humans are attending in a cocktail party like scene would empower applications in brain computer interfaces and assistive devices such as hearing aids. Here we demonstrate that, in an overt attention task, the attended spatial location can be decoded robustly from single trial hemodynamic responses, using a whole head high density fNIRS system. We also identify critical brain regions that make the highest contribution to decoding accuracy. Specifically, we find that decoding based on a small fraction of channels located within the left and right inferior parietal lobule (IPL) achieves maximal decoding accuracy comparable to all channels. Decoding fell close to chance in a covert auditory condition in which participants held central fixation while attending to the same talkers, indicating that auditory attention alone without orientation is not sufficient for decoding. Finally, control experiments suggest that overt-condition decoding is influenced by sustained eye position/gaze direction, not eye movement. These results support the development of fNIRS-integrated BCIs and assistive devices controlled by overt spatial attention.

item.title: Basic-level category processing advantage in fear generalization and its modulation by threat-conditioned stimulus diversity: Behavioral and event-related potential evidence.
item.description:
Behaviour research and therapy
Category-based fear generalization refers to the extension of acquired fear responses to novel stimuli sharing categorical cues with a threat stimulus. Categories are organized into superordinate, basic-level, and subordinate levels, which differ in cognitive processing advantages; however, whether this categorical advantage influences fear generalization remains unclear. Experiment 1 used a discriminative fear conditioning paradigm, employing subordinate exemplars of birds and measuring tools as the threat-conditioned stimulus (CS+) and the safety-conditioned stimulus (CS-), respectively. During the generalization test, we included generalization stimuli sharing either the same basic-level category (GSBasic ) or the same superordinate category (but different basic-level category) as the CS+. Fear generalization was assessed via shock expectancy ratings and skin conductance responses. Experiment 2 manipulated CS+ diversity (high vs. low) in the same task while recording electroencephalography to examine its moderating role. Behaviorally, acquired fear generalized more robustly to GSBasic than to GS sharing the same superordinate category (GSSuperordinate ). Participants in the high-diversity group showed higher shock expectancy ratings for both the CS+ and GSBasic than those in the low-diversity group. Event-related potential results revealed that GSBasic elicited P2 and N400 amplitudes comparable to those of the CS+, and exhibited more positive P2 and less negative N400 amplitudes than GSSuperordinate and CS-. Moreover, only the CS+ and GSBasic elicited more positive LPP amplitudes than CS-. These findings suggest that early attentional allocation, late semantic processing, and motivational attention collectively constitute the electrophysiological basis of the basic-level category processing advantage in fear generalization, offering implications for the intervention of anxiety disorders.

item.title: Reversal of refractory epilepsy in an adult with GAMT deficiency: A case report and comparative literature review.
item.description:
Epilepsia open
Objective Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive creatine biosynthesis disorder. Reports specifically focusing on adult patients remain scarce. Methods We report a 52-year-old female (the oldest documented case of GAMT deficiency to date) presenting with severe intellectual disability, refractory epilepsy, and adult-onset disease progression. Whole-exome sequencing identified novel compound heterozygous GAMT variants (c.265_267del and c.253G>T), and magnetic resonance spectroscopy confirmed cerebral creatine depletion. Remarkably, initiating oral creatine supplementation at age 52 achieved complete seizure freedom, normalization of the electroencephalogram (EEG), and significant motor function recovery. Results A comprehensive review revealed that untreated adult patients face a high risk of progressive neurological deterioration. Compared to the pediatric cohort, adults exhibited a significantly higher prevalence of movement disorders (69.2% vs. 33.1%, p < 0.001) and a trend toward a higher prevalence of epilepsy (92.3% vs. 74.2%). Especially, atonic seizures (drop attacks) are particularly characteristic of adult GAMT deficiency, with EEGs frequently demonstrating background slowing, multifocal epileptiform discharges, and electrodecremental patterns. Significance This study underscores that continuous disease progression and prolonged neurotoxicity still could compromise the well-being of adult GAMT deficiency patients. Accurate diagnosis is essential for adults presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) phenotype, as even late treatment for GAMT deficiency can still dramatically alleviate the epileptic burden and reverse motor decline. Plain language summary We report the oldest known adult diagnosed with GAMT deficiency. Our case demonstrates that starting creatine treatment even at age 52 can dramatically reduce seizures and restore motor function. Literature shows that untreated adults suffer from more severe epilepsy and movement disorders than children, with symptoms worsening over time. These findings highlight the critical need for genetic testing in adults with unexplained severe epilepsy; timely creatine supplementation can halt cognitive decline and significantly restore quality of life.

item.title: Speech Tracking in fMRI Reveals a Distinct Response to Sentence Boundaries During Comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Psycholinguistic research and linguistic theory suggest that comprehending continuous speech involves segmenting it into sentences. Yet, direct neuroimaging evidence for this process remains scarce, partly because sentence boundaries coincide with acoustic, prosodic, lexical, and syntactic changes. Here, we used whole-brain fMRI to test whether sentence boundaries elicit a neural response beyond these accompanying speech properties during spontaneous speech comprehension. We modelled BOLD responses to sentence-final words alongside continuous regressors characterizing accompanying speech properties. This approach revealed sensitivity to continuously varying features of speech across multiple brain regions. Notably, the acoustic envelope predicted BOLD responses in bilateral primary auditory cortices. Responses associated with prosodic breaks and emphasis were found in right temporal cortex, syntactic bottom-up node count in the left superior temporal sulcus, and word concreteness in the parahippocampal gyri. Critically, sentence-final words were associated with an increased activation in right temporal regions, after accounting for acoustic, prosodic, lexical, semantic and syntactic properties. These findings provide evidence for a neural response to sentence boundaries consistent with active sentence segmentation. More generally, this study demonstrates the value of continuous-regressor modelling for investigating speech comprehension with fMRI.

item.title: Time at Home for Whom? Unequal Returns of Paid Family Leave for Infant White Matter and Language Development
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Paid family leave (PFL) may give parents more time with infants, ease financial strain, and support stable routines. Although PFL has been linked to child development, little is known about neural pathways that might underpin its benefits or whether associations vary across families. Using data from 274 infants in the HEALthy Brain and Child Development Study, we examined associations of maternal and paternal PFL with language ability at 12 months and white matter microstructure at 6 months. We tested whether associations varied by the corresponding parent’s education. Neither maternal nor paternal PFL was directly associated with language scores or fractional anisotropy in the left arcuate, inferior longitudinal, or uncinate fasciculus. Maternal education moderated associations between maternal PFL and fractional anisotropy in the arcuate ( p = .014) and inferior longitudinal fasciculus ( p = .003; n = 148). In both tracts, PFL was associated with higher fractional anisotropy only among infants whose mothers had relatively high education. No comparable pattern emerged for language, the uncinate fasciculus, or paternal PFL. Findings suggest that the neurodevelopmental correlates of PFL may depend on family resources rather than operate uniformly across families, underscoring the need to pair paid leave with additional supports and resources. Lay Summary Paid family leave may give parents more time at home, steadier daily routines, and less financial worry in the months after a birth, all of which could change the care an infant receives. But these benefits may not be equal across families. In a national study of infants, we examined whether paid leave taken by mothers, fathers or partners was related to early language skills and to the organization of brain pathways involved in language. Paid leave was not directly related to language scores or brain development overall. However, maternal paid leave was associated with more mature organization in two language-related brain pathways only among infants whose mothers had higher levels of education. No similar pattern was found for father or partner leave. These findings suggest that paid leave alone may not reduce early developmental disparities, and that policies offering paid leave may need to be paired with additional support for families with fewer resources.

item.title: Movie Watching for Individual Functional Brain Network Estimation in Adolescents
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
SUMMARY Precision functional mapping (PFM) reveals stable individual differences in brain functional network organization and holds promise for advancing neuropsychiatric clinical care. PFM requires sufficient high-quality and densely sampled functional MRI data at the individual level that is typically acquired during the so-called resting state while passively fixating on a crosshair. However, crosshair fixation acquisitions can be challenging especially for pediatric or patient populations, where alternatives like movie watching might be used to improve data quality and reduce participant burden. Here, we compare the use of resting state crosshair fixation and movie watching fMRI data to derive individual-specific functional brain network topography using PFM data (28–38 minutes of low-motion fMRI data per-participant per-condition) in nineteen adolescents (12-18 years) with a range of transdiagnostic psychiatric diagnoses. Network assignments were largely conserved between crosshair fixation and movie watching, with a smaller subset of reproducible network reassignments which were overwhelmingly border shifts between neighboring networks. This suggests largely conserved global structure of functional network topography between crosshair fixation and movie watching, though border shifts can compound into variable estimates of cortical network size particularly for movie positive (language, salience, and parietal memory) and movie negative networks (default mode, action mode). Functional network assignments derived from movies and crosshair were also similarly individual-specific and consistent within common neuromodulation targets including dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and somatomotor cortex. Key results were replicated in independent pediatric consortia data (Healthy Brain Network, n = 466, 6-22 years) and reproduced across independent PFM data sessions. Acknowledging individual differences and level of analysis, we conclude that movies are a viable alternative to resting state crosshair fixation for individual network definitions.

item.title: Concordance and Association of Kidokoro MRI Scores at 32 and 40 Weeks Postmenstrual Age with Neurodevelopmental Outcomes in Very Preterm Infants.
item.description:
AJNR. American journal of neuroradiology
Background and purpose Early identification of neurodevelopmental risk in very preterm infants is critical for timely intervention. The Kidokoro MRI scoring system offers a semiquantitative approach to evaluating brain abnormalities. This study aimed to assess the agreement of Kidokoro scores obtained in the same infants at 32 and 40 weeks postmenstrual age, and their association to cognitive, language, and motor outcomes at 24 months corrected age. Materials and methods A cohort of 187 very preterm infants (median 28+5 weeks gestational age; 55% boys) underwent structural MRI at 2 time points: early (median 32+2 weeks) and term-equivalent age (TEA; median 40+5 weeks), using 3T scanners. Scans were scored independently using a modified version of the Kidokoro system. Bland-Altman analysis assessed agreement between early and TEA scores. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were assessed at 24 months using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition (Bayley-III). Multivariable linear regression models evaluated the predictive value of MRI scores, adjusting for sex, gestational age, birth weight centile, and socioeconomic status. Results Early MRI scores were consistently higher than TEA scores (mean difference: 1.9; 95% CI, 1.6-2.2), with WM scores showing the largest discrepancy (mean difference: 1.68; 95% CI, 1.46-1.90), primarily due to the myelination delay item. Excluding this item reduced the difference to 0.32 (95% CI, -0.01 to 0.64). Early and TEA Kidokoro Global Brain Abnormality Score (GBAS) were negatively associated with Bayley-III cognitive and motor, but not language scores. Higher GBAS were associated with lower cognitive (early: β = -0.67 [95% CI, -1.23 to -0.11], partial R 2 = 0.03; TEA: β = -0.60 [95% CI, -1.15 to -0.06], partial R 2 = 0.03) and motor scores (early: β = -1.04 [95% CI, -1.67 to -0.41], partial R 2 = 0.06; TEA: β = -1.18 [95% CI, -1.78 to -0.58], partial R 2 = 0.08). Reduction in GBAS from early to TEA correlated with higher motor scores (β = 1.02 [95% CI, 0.03-2.02], partial R 2 = 0.02). WM abnormalities were linked to poorer motor outcomes at both time points. Conclusions Kidokoro scores at early and term-equivalent time points are associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes at 24 months. Global abnormalities and WM scored at either time points, or their longitudinal changes are significantly linked to motor outcomes. Refinement of the scoring system for the early assessment may enhance clinical utility.

item.title: Functional and Structural Imaging Features of Cognitive Profiles in Multiple Sclerosis.
item.description:
Neurology(R) neuroimmunology & neuroinflammation
Background and objectives Cognitive impairment affects 40%-70% of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS). Although recent hypothesis-driven and data-driven efforts have identified cognitive phenotypes, functional substrates underlying impairment in such phenotypes are still not clear. Our objective was to identify distinct cognitive phenotypes using clustering in a large cohort of patients with MS and characterize their associated clinical, structural MRI, and resting-state (RS) functional connectivity (FC) features. Methods We conducted an observational, cross-sectional study with right-handed patients with MS and age-matched and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs) who underwent neurologic and neuropsychological evaluation (Brief Repeatable Battery of Neuropsychological tests). Latent profile analysis on cognitive test Z-scores identified MS cognitive phenotypes. 3.0T MRI was used to derive atrophy measures and RS FC within default mode network (DMN I/II), executive control network (ECN), left/right fronto-parietal, language, and salience networks. Linear regression models compared structural MRI and RS FC across cognitive phenotypes and HCs, while polynomial contrasts assessed RS FC patterns across groups. Results Three hundred and sixty-nine patients with MS and 168 HCs were enrolled. Four cognitive phenotypes were detected: preserved cognition ([PC], n = 67[18.2%]), mild single-domain verbal fluency involvement (MSD-VF, n = 37[10.0%]), mild single-domain attention involvement (MSD-A, n = 197[53.4%]), and severe multidomain (SMD) involvement (SMD, n = 68[18.4%]). At corrected threshold, PC patients showed decreased deep gray matter (GM) volumes (p < 0.001-0.001) and similar RS FC vs HCs, whereas MSD-VF exhibited no significant atrophy and no differences in RS FC vs HCs. MSD-A displayed lower cortical/deep GM volumes vs HCs (p < 0.001-0.005), whereas SMD had worse clinical and atrophy features (p < 0.001-0.04), as well as decreased DMN II RS FC (p = 0.01-0.04) vs other groups. Polynomial contrast analyses revealed significant quadratic patterns with increased RS FC in MSD-VF vs HC/PC groups, followed by decrease in MSD-A and SMD, within DMN II (p = 0.005), ECN (p = 0.005), and language network (p < 0.001). Discussion PC exhibited intact RS FC, whereas SMD presented widespread structural and DMN RS FC damage. These findings advance our understanding of cognitive heterogeneity in MS by revealing distinct structural and functional neuroimaging profiles across cognitive phenotypes, encouraging future longitudinal and multimodal investigations to improve disease characterization and prognostic stratification.
